title: Japan raises rates to 1.25% as producer costs begin reaching households
summary: The September 18 meeting raised the uncollateralized overnight call-rate guideline from about 1.0% to about 1.25%. The Board voted 7–2 on both the guideline and the facility rates that implement it. The complementary deposit facility would pay 1.25% on eligible balances and the complementary lending facility would charge 1.5%. All three changes would take effect on September 24. Announcement and implementation therefore fall on different trading dates. The Bank justified acting before CPI excluding fresh food reached 2% by pointing to emerging pass-through, rising inflation expectations and financial conditions it still considered accommodative (sections 1–2 and 4).

This was a change in where cost pressures were visible. Producers continued to report high year-on-year price increases, reflecting more expensive oil, a weaker yen and demand for AI-related products. The Bank saw these business-to-business costs beginning to reach consumers. Wages were also being passed through into selling prices. CPI excluding fresh food had recently risen moderately into a 1.5–2.0% range, even with measures supporting household energy bills. Underlying inflation was approaching 2% in the majority’s assessment. That assessment relied on broad price and wage behaviour. The document supplies neither a single measured underlying rate nor a rule linking the next hike to the next CPI print (section 4 and attachment).

International technology demand mattered for both sides of Japan’s economy. Exports and industrial production had started increasing moderately and corporate profits remained high. Higher semiconductor prices and the yen’s earlier depreciation could raise retail durable-goods prices. Increased oil costs could weaken real incomes at the same time. Construction costs affected fixed investment, while housing investment continued to decline. Private consumption was resilient despite weakness in household sentiment. The Board consequently saw sufficient underlying activity to sustain the wage-price cycle, with an uneven distribution of gains and costs across households and firms (attachment, sections 1–2).

The outlook projected CPI excluding fresh food clearly above 2% from the second half of fiscal 2026 before earlier cost effects faded. It expected underlying inflation to become broadly consistent with target between the second half of fiscal 2026 and fiscal 2027, and subsequently to remain around that level. The Board was concerned that a shift toward repeated price and wage increases might instead push the underlying rate above target. It retained a direction of travel toward higher rates, with timing and pace dependent on incoming activity, prices and financial conditions. Negative consequences of an eventual overshoot weighed in that judgment alongside the immediate cost of more expensive borrowing (sections 4–5 and attachment).

The vote reveals disagreement in both directions. Toichiro Asada preferred a hold, emphasizing sub-2% inflation excluding fresh food and uncertainty about the strength of activity. Ayano Sato also wanted to hold, seeing little evidence of substantial acceleration. Conversely, Hajime Takata and Naoki Tamura supported tightening but separately challenged the outlook’s assessment of timing. Both judged underlying inflation to have broadly reached a target-consistent rate already. A record of two dissenters captures the disagreement over the current instrument. It misses the additional two members who thought the Bank’s characterization of inflation was behind the data (decision voting note and attachment note).

Credit supply remained favourable in the majority’s account. Real rates were low over much of the short and medium range, loan demand was growing and lenders remained willing to supply funds. Commercial paper and corporate bond issuance conditions were also favourable. Separately, the Board unanimously switched the climate-support lending operation to a floating rate and introduced borrowing limits. The change affects the terms on which participating institutions finance eligible activity. An aggregate credit measure could obscure a shift specific to institutions using the facility (sections 3–4).

The release was published at 11:54 Japan time. Measure any announcement surprise against market expectations immediately beforehand. Use September 24 separately to examine whether the effective overnight market rate and remuneration on eligible balances moved into line with the new operating parameters. Repricing in Japanese government bonds or the yen over the intervening days could include oil, foreign rates or other news. The size of the 25-basis-point policy move sets no mechanical prediction for these prices (footnotes 1–2 and release reference).

questions.question: How much of the increase had markets priced before 11:54?
questions.detail: Compare the pre-announcement distribution of expected policy rates with meeting-dated overnight-indexed swap repricing in the first minutes after release. Separate the current decision from changes in forwards covering later meetings. Use actual overnight transactions on September 24 to test implementation rather than mixing the effective-date rate change into the announcement return.

questions.question: Was the rise in producer costs becoming broad-based domestic inflation?
questions.detail: Match import and producer prices to consumer categories with plausible lags and track wages alongside prices in labour-intensive services. Distinguish semiconductor-intensive durables, oil-sensitive goods and government-supported energy. A retail increase concentrated in imported products would have a different implication for underlying persistence from synchronized repricing in domestic services.

questions.question: Did the hike tighten credit most for households and firms outside the AI expansion?
questions.detail: Compare lending rates, borrowing volumes, survey credit conditions and debt-service costs by firm size and sector. Allow for floating-rate contracts and different repricing dates. Examine whether profits, output and demand for funds in technology-related activity mask financing pressure among housing borrowers, small importers or domestically oriented businesses.
